item.title: Asylum: applications drop in Switzerland in 2026
item.description: In the first half of 2026, for the first time since 2022, fewer than 10,000 requests were received. The SEM revises downwards: from 26,000 to 22,000 annual applications.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - In the first half of 2026, asylum applications fell below 10,000 for the first time since 2022 - The Confederation revises downwards the estimates: from 26,000 to 22,000 requests for the entire year - The decrease mainly concerns Afghan, Turkish and Eritrean applicants - Applications for S (Ukrainian) status drop to about 12,000 in 2026
## Key facts - What: Marked drop in the number of asylum applications registered in Switzerland in 2026 - When: First semester 2026 (less than 10,000 applications); full year forecast - Where: Switzerland - Who: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM); Afghan, Turkish, Eritrean, Ukrainian applicants - Revised estimates: from 26,000 to 22,000 requests in 2026 - Articles of Association S: 12,000 expected by the end of 2026 (decrease of about 900 vs 2025) - Reasons: Decrease in Mediterranean crossings and Balkan route
Asylum applications continue to decline in Switzerland. In the first half of 2026, for the first time since the beginning of 2022, fewer than 10,000 applications were registered. A signal that prompted the Confederation to significantly revise the annual forecasts: the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) announced that the total applications for 2026 will be 22,000 instead of the 26,000 initially estimated.
### The collapse of questions in the first semester
The downward trend is now consolidated. In the first half of 2026, the number of applications fell below the threshold of 10,000 units, a figure that had not been recorded since 2022. The downward revision of the Geopolitical dynamics and European migration flows largely explain this structural decline. The downward trend in Mediterranean crossings is not an isolated phenomenon in Switzerland, but involves all of Western Europe, where stricter controls and search and rescue operations continuously change available routes. The reduction of those using the Balkan route also signals a different balance in migration incentives and opportunities perceived by asylum seekers in various transit and destination countries.
### Countries of origin and the weight of new balances
The decline concentrated on Afghans, Turks, and Eritreans is not coincidental. These three countries were historically among the main countries of origin for asylum seekers in Switzerland. The decrease in applications from these contexts signals that migration pressures are reorienting towards other European destinations, or that conditions at departure are changing. Factors such as perceived stability in countries of origin, local economic opportunities, or changes in regional conflicts directly influence flows reaching Swiss territory.
In the case of Ukrainians, the number of applications for S status decreases progressively. The SEM expects 12,000 requests by end of 2026, about 900 fewer than in 2025. This reflects the evolution of the Ukrainian situation and the diversified strategies that Ukrainian refugees adopt: voluntary repatriation to Ukraine as areas stabilize, or relocation to other European countries. S status, while remaining an effective protection instrument, has exhausted the peak of applications from the first months of the crisis.
For those receiving refugee status, [integration into the Swiss labor market](nav:jobs) represents a priority in the integration process in the cantons.
### Implications for cantonal and federal policies
The decline in applications has direct repercussions on the territorial distribution of asylum seekers. Cantonal authorities, responsible for receiving and integrating applicants after the federal examination phase, will be able to count on lower numbers compared to the year's initial forecasts. This creates breathing room for reception and accommodation services, reducing pressure on dedicated facilities and allowing better quality support at the local level. The cantons will be able to reallocate resources towards integration services, language training, and job placement for applicants already present on the territory.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How the asylum application process works in Switzerland
Anyone wishing to apply for asylum in Switzerland must submit an application to a reception office of the State Secretariat for Migration. The procedure follows a structured process: initial registration with collection of personal data, formal examination of the application based on criteria established by Swiss federal law, possible hearing with an official in charge of the investigation, and finally official decision regarding approval or rejection. During the examination process, which can last for months, applicants receive accommodation in dedicated facilities managed by federal entities and a small daily allowance for living expenses. Once the SEM has issued the decision, the file passes to the cantons, which become responsible for reception, accommodation, and integration in the local territory if refugee status or provisional admission status has been granted.
### Cantonal planning and employment opportunities
For 2026, given the lower number of expected applications (22,000 instead of 26,000), the cantons will be able to plan reception resources proportionate to this revised figure. The SEM provides operational guidance to the cantons and coordinates the territorial distribution of applicants according to criteria for balance among the various local entities. Those who receive refugee status can immediately access the Swiss labor market in all professions, except for specific exclusions on security grounds. They will also be able to benefit from cantonal social benefits according to local legislation. The reduction of 4,000 annual applications compared to initial estimates means that reception spaces, social workers, and cantonal integration services will be able to dedicate greater attention to the quality of support rather than managing emergency volumes.
### Monitoring and future adjustments
The SEM will continue to carefully monitor flows during the rest of 2026. Any further variations in European migration routes, control policies adopted by neighboring states, or global geopolitical balances could further modify the actual figures. However, the downward trend appears consolidated for the near future. The cantons have already begun communicating with each other and with the SEM to adjust multi-year reception plans based on the new official estimates.
For asylum seekers who obtain protection status, the success of integration also depends on access to employment. [Discover which companies are hiring](nav:companies) and what concrete opportunities exist in the Swiss labor market. A decline in applications creates less friction in integration services and allows for more personalized professional support pathways, to the benefit of better quality integration in the cantons.

item.title: Buying a house Bern: prices, mortgage and documents
item.description: Buying a house in Bern: the Swiss legal framework, mortgage loans, transfer taxes and notary fees illustrated in a practical guide for buyers.
item.content:encoded:
## At a glance - Swiss tax system at 3 levels: federal, cantonal, municipal - Transfer tax is cantonal responsibility, varies by canton - Mortgage: banks require minimum 20% own funds - Mandatory notarial procedure and federal land registration
## Key facts - **What**: Property sale regulated by federal law (CO) and cantonal taxes - Where: Canton of Bern; cantonal tax and administrative jurisdiction - Who: Buyer, seller, notary, bank, cantonal land registry - Legal basis: Code of Obligations (CO) art. 214 et seq. - Mandatory intervention: Notary for deed validity and registration
The purchase of a residential property in Switzerland is regulated by a uniform federal legal framework and variable cantonal taxes. In the Canton of Bern, as in every canton, the purchase of real estate property entails compliance with procedures defined by the Code of Obligations (CO), the intervention of an authorized notary, and the payment of transfer taxes determined by Bernese cantonal legislation.
### Legal framework for real estate property
Real estate property in Switzerland is regulated by federal law, which ensures uniformity in registration procedures and the recognition of property rights throughout the national territory. Cantonal law, on the other hand, defines the taxes due at the time of property transfer — transfer tax — and municipal multipliers, which vary significantly from canton to canton and from municipality to municipality.
In the Canton of Bern, the cantonal administration manages the Land Registry (Grundbuch), a public instrument that certifies land ownership and registers immovable property rights. When you purchase a home in Bern, the property does not officially become yours until the notarial deed is registered in the cantonal Land Registry. This procedure ensures legal certainty and transparency in the Swiss real estate market.
The intervention of a notary is mandatory for the legal validity of the purchase deed. The notary, a professional figure regulated at the cantonal level, drafts the contract according to federal regulations, verifies the identity of the parties, holds the funds during the transaction, and registers the document with the Land Registry. To learn more about the national tax system, consult our tax calculation tool.
### Transfer taxes and costs in property transfer
Transfer tax — the tax due upon transfer of real estate property — is the exclusive responsibility of cantons in Switzerland. In the Canton of Bern, the tax rate and calculation methods are defined by Bernese legislation and vary significantly compared to other Swiss cantons. There is no uniform federal transfer tax; each canton independently decides whether to introduce such a tax and at what rate.
Notarial fees, on the other hand, follow a uniform federal procedure. The notary charges a fee proportionate to the property value, according to rates regulated by the cantons. In the Canton of Bern, there is an official schedule of notarial fees that ensures cost transparency and uniformity among professionals.
In addition to transfer tax, the buyer must consider other costs in the property transaction: land registration fees with the cantonal administration, administrative fees, mandatory insurance (fire insurance for mortgaged properties), and potentially independent real estate appraisal expenses. [For a comprehensive overview of investment costs in Switzerland, discover our cost of living tool.](nav:cost-of-living) Purchasing a property in Bern, as throughout Switzerland, requires solid financial planning and understanding of banking requirements. Most buyers resort to a mortgage, a financing secured by the property itself. Understanding standard banking requirements and assessing the financial sustainability of the mortgage is essential before proceeding with the signing of the deed of sale.
### The Swiss mortgage: structure and banking requirements
In Switzerland, banks generally require borrowers to have a minimum of 20% of the property value as own funds paid in. The remaining 80% is financed through the mortgage. This requirement is an established banking practice throughout the country and aims to reduce the risk of default, protecting both the credit institution and the buyer.
The Swiss mortgage is typically structured in two distinct levels. The first mortgage (first rank) usually represents up to 65-70% of the property value and carries the lowest risk for the bank, with more favorable interest rates. The second mortgage (second rank) covers the portion between the first mortgage and 80% of the total value, and has a generally higher interest rate since it carries greater risk for the credit institution.
Interest rates on mortgages vary depending on the general economic situation, the policies of the Swiss National Bank (SNB) and the commercial strategies of individual banks. There is no uniform national rate; each credit institution independently sets its own rates based on the buyer's risk profile and current market conditions. [Use our mortgage calculator to estimate your financing capacity.](nav:calculator)
### Mortgage sustainability: the 33% rule
The financial sustainability of the mortgage is a crucial aspect that Swiss banks carefully assess before granting financing. Banks apply an established rule of thumb: the annual mortgage cost (capital plus interest) should not exceed 33% of the borrower's gross annual income. This threshold ensures that the borrower does not expose themselves to excessive risk of default if personal or market economic conditions change.
To assess sustainability, the bank requires the mortgage applicant to submit their pay slip, federal tax declarations for recent years, and sometimes a complete statement of assets. On this basis, the credit institution calculates the repayment capacity and decides whether to grant the mortgage and in what maximum amount.
A hypothetical scenario illustrates the concept: if a buyer has a gross annual income of CHF 100,000, the bank considers sustainable an annual mortgage payment of no more than CHF 33,000 (approximately CHF 2,750 per month). This calculation assumes stable market conditions and interest rates over time. If the buyer's personal economic situation changes (income reduction, job loss) or if interest rates increase significantly, the bank may request a renegotiation of the mortgage or a reduction of the financed amount.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### House Purchase Procedure in Bern: The Main Phases
The process of purchasing a residential property follows a standardized sequence at the federal level, although administrative and tax details vary by canton. In the Canton of Bern, the process is governed by the Code of Obligations (CO) and cantonal laws relating to land registry registration and transfer taxes. Understanding the main steps of the procedure allows you to properly plan the timing, costs, and responsibilities of the transaction.
Phase 1: Property Search and Purchase Offer The buyer identifies the property of interest and submits a verbal or written purchase offer to the seller. This initial offer is not yet legally binding; both parties can negotiate the terms of the transaction (price, transfer date, special conditions).
Phase 2: Preliminary Verification and Mortgage Pre-approval Once the preliminary offer is accepted, the buyer should conduct thorough checks: - Obtain an independent property appraisal (optional but strongly recommended) - Verify certificates and entries in the cantonal Land Registry - Check for any encumbrances, mortgages, or servitudes existing on the property - Ensure the availability of a pre-approved mortgage from your trusted bank
Phase 3: Execution of the Notarial Deed The notary, upon instruction from the parties, drafts the purchase and sale deed based on the concluded negotiations. The deed contains a detailed description of the property (location, areas, attached rights), the purchase price, payment terms, the transfer date and all agreed conditions. Both parties sign the deed in the presence of an authorized notary, guaranteeing the authenticity and legal validity of the document under federal law.
Phase 4: Registration in the Cantonal Land Registry The notary transmits the deed to the competent cantonal administration (Land Registry Office of the Canton of Bern) for official registration. Once registered in the public Land Registry, the property officially transfers to the buyer and their ownership right is inscribed by law.
Phase 5: Payment and Final Settlement The buyer pays the purchase price, the cantonal transfer tax, notarial fees and all other costs due according to the schedule established in the notarial deed. The bank disburses the mortgage directly to the notary or buyer, who proceeds with payment at the times agreed by the parties.
### Buyer Checklist: Documents and Preparation
Before proceeding with the purchase of a residential property, verify you have available: - Mortgage pre-approval certificate from the bank (or confirmation of availability of sufficient personal funds) - Personal funds available equal to at least 20% of the estimated value of the property - Complete personal documentation (passport or ID card, current employment contracts, bank statements) - Certificate of personal solvency (solvency booklet) required by most Swiss banks - Consultation with an accountant or independent tax advisor (recommended to assess personal and cantonal tax implications)
The residential property purchase procedure in Switzerland is protected by federal and cantonal laws that guarantee legal transparency and certainty in transactions. For specific questions about the procedure in the Canton of Bern, contact the cantonal Land Registry Office, the Bernese Cantonal Tax Administration, or a notary authorized by the canton.
### Next Steps: Calculate and Compare
Use Frontaliere Ticino's mortgage sustainability calculator to estimate the maximum financing amount you could access based on your gross income and standard Swiss banking requirements. Carefully compare mortgage offers from different banks — interest rates and conditions vary significantly between financial institutions — and consult a real estate law specialist for a complete review of the purchase documents before notarial signature.

item.title: Artificial intelligence: 80% of Swiss use it
item.description: 80% of the Swiss use AI. Doubled in two years according to IGEM-Digimonitor. YouTube 80%, Instagram 45%, X drops to 10%.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - 80% of the Swiss population uses AI - Doubled usage in two years - Radio loses audience to streaming - X (ex Twitter) drops from 17% to 10%
- **What**: Study on the digital behaviour of the Swiss population - When: Recent survey - Where: Switzerland - Who: IGEM-Digimonitor and WEMF AG für Werbemedienforschung - AI diffusion: 80% of the population - Trend: Use doubled in two years
Artificial intelligence is spreading in Switzerland at an accelerated pace. According to the IGEM-Digimonitor and WEMF AG survey on media research and advertising, 80% of the Swiss population now uses AI in both [sul posto di lavoro](nav:jobs) and in the private sector. The figure represents a doubling compared to just two years ago, with particularly high prevalence between the ages of 15 and 24.
AI applications go beyond texts and translations. Information research, consultancy for purchases and e-learning are now established fields of use. In online research, 77% of respondents employ AI mode integrated into classic search engines, while 57% access dedicated AI platforms. This makes AI platforms more used than YouTube (34% per search) and social media (28%).
### Television resists, streaming advances
The television holds its position firmly. 92% of the population uses TV offers at least occasionally, and 54% watch it every day. In parallel, streaming conquers space: 47% Social media now plays multiple roles in the daily lives of the Swiss, far beyond the original entertainment.
### Social Media: The Expanding Role
Two-thirds of the population uses social networks on a daily basis. If the use is lower in German Switzerland and among the ultra-55-year-olds, social networks are integrated into the lives of the youngest. In addition to fun, more than half of the population uses them as a news channel. 44% also use them for e-learning, accessing educational content. Between the ages of 15-34, social networks play a decisive role in the search for information and purchase advice.
Social commerce (direct purchase via social media) remains marginal: 18% of the population practices it.
### Platforms: the new balance between generations
Instagram holds the record: 45% of the population uses it on a daily basis. Facebook follows with 26%, Snapchat with 16% and TikTok with 14%. X (formerly Twitter) suffered a marked contraction, collapsing from 17% in 2024 to 10% in 2026.
However, younger generations show radically different preferences. Between the ages of 15 and 34, Instagram reaches 72% of daily use, Snapchat 44% and TikTok 31%. This gap highlights how very young people adopt platforms that diverge from those of the general population. For the [aziende e i brand svizzeri](nav:companies), this fragmentation poses significant challenges in digital communication, requiring multichannel strategies
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Digital skills as a priority
The explosion in the use of AI (doubled in two years) and the change in digital behaviours put continuing education back at the centre of the work and personal agenda. Those who work or are looking for work in Switzerland should consider digital skills not as optional, but as a core element. 80% of the population now uses AI on a daily basis at work, which means that the vast majority of jobs offer or will require at least a basic familiarity with these tools.
### How to keep up
You don't need to become an AI expert - just understand the fundamentals and know how to use it ethically. Online training opportunities proliferate — from university platforms to business courses — and many courses are accessible for free or at low cost. If you are an employee, check if your employer offers internal AI training; if you are self-employed, invest in refresher courses.
Checking in regularly on how your industry or sector adopts AI is crucial. The study data shows that AI now permeates online search (77% in classic engines, 57% on dedicated platforms), which means that tools and best practices are constantly changing. item.title: Neutrality initiative weakens Switzerland's role
item.description: An alliance of 22 organisations warns that approval of the neutrality initiative would result in disengagement from international law and weaken Switzerland's position in promoting peace.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Alliance of 22 organisations opposes Swiss neutrality initiative - The initiative looks to the past, not to the peace of tomorrow, says Günther Bächler - Risk of Switzerland becoming a platform for circumventing economic sanctions - Created Politopia.ch, a simulator to assess the impact of the initiative
## Key facts - **What**: Swiss neutrality initiative opposed by alliance of 22 organizations - When: Ongoing debate; recently launched Politopia.ch simulator - Where: Switzerland — federal politics, diplomacy and international law - Who: Amnesty International, Alliance F, Operation Free, Public Eye, Alliance South + experts (Bächler, Keller, Bachmann, Marchon) - Impact: Weakening of Switzerland's international credibility and mediation capacity - Tool: Politopia.ch allows you to evaluate the consequences of the initiative
### The Opposition Front
An alliance of 22 non-governmental organizations launched a campaign to oppose the Swiss neutrality initiative, saying that its approval would have serious consequences for Switzerland's foreign policy and international role. Promoters include Amnesty International, Alliance F, Operation Free, Public Eye and Alliance South, which coordinated a unified response.
Günther Bächler, former Swiss diplomat and international mediator for peace, summed up the main criticism during a conference ### International credibility and the paradox of neutrality
Switzerland's position as a mediator in international law rests on two seemingly contradictory pillars: formal neutrality on the one hand and membership in an international democratic community on the other. The neutrality initiative seeks to reinforce the first pillar, but according to the alliance it would have the paradoxical effect of weakening both.
Switzerland retains its credibility as a mediator only if it remains integrated into international networks and if it positions itself as a reliable member of a democratic community founded on international law. Extreme neutrality, interpreted as total abstention from any sanctioning action, would make the whole world suspect that Switzerland is not reliable when it really needs it.
The paradox is obvious: a country that refuses to act in the face of international crimes is not neutral in the positive sense, but simply complicit in inaction. Lisa Marchon, co-president of Opération Libero, puts it in clear terms: "Security comes from cooperation with democratic partners, not from impunity." In other words, the security of Switzerland itself depends on the functioning of an international system based on rules and responsibilities.

The neutrality initiative will follow the standard Swiss procedural process. After signature collection, the text will be submitted to a popular vote. At that point, all Swiss residents with the right to vote will be able to express themselves on the matter.

item.title: Army, the compromise on financing
item.description: The Finance Commission proposes a fund with debt of up to 6 billion per year from 2027. Financing: VAT +0.2%, credit residuals and surpluses 2026. Voting in September and December 2026.

The Finance Commission of the Council of States has reached a compromise on the army's request for additional funds at short notice. The dossier now goes to the Federal Parliament for the final vote and represents a significant step forward in the Swiss defence debate.
The solution envisioned by the Government remains that of an ad hoc fund for the army, authorized to borrow to advance military investments without binding it to ordinary federal budget cycles. The maximum limit: 6 billion francs per year from 2027.

For an average Swiss family with annual consumer spending, we talk about small amounts per single purchase, but the effect accumulates over time and affects the overall cost of living.
VAT in Switzerland includes three rates: 8.1% (standard), 2.5% (essential goods such as food), 3.7% (hospitality and catering). The timeframe is tight. The military has expressed the urgency of advancing investments before global prices rise further. If Parliament passes the law but the people vote no in a referendum, the fund would be dissolved and a new financing would have to start from scratch.
### What citizens and businesses should do
Residents of Switzerland do not have immediate action to take. However:
If VAT increases, it is advisable to advance purchases of durable goods (cars, furniture, large appliances) before 2027 to avoid additional tax burden. Those working in Switzerland who track deductible expenses (freelancers, SMEs) will need to recalculate their fixed cost structure.
If the referendum blocks the plan, the government will have to return to Parliament with a new draft law, probably by 2027-2028. In this case, military investments will suffer further delays.

Parliamentary votes and official results will be published on the website of the Federal Parliament (parlament.ch) and the Federal Chancellery (admin.ch). The full text of the law will be available in public legislative portals.
The decision of the Finance Commission represents a significant step toward funding the Swiss military, but the Swiss democratic process — Parliament + possible referendum — ensures that the final word remains with the citizens.

item.title: Buying a house in Bern: prices, mortgage and taxes
item.description: Guide to real estate purchase costs in the Canton of Bern: mortgage loan, own funds, transfer taxes and notary fees for those who buy a house in Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Required own funds: 20% of the purchase price (Swiss standard) - Mortgage loans: from 15 to 20 years, variable rates with the decisions of the SNB - Transfer taxes: vary per canton (specific for Bern at the Cantonal Office) - Notary fees: 0.1%-0.3% of the purchase price
## Key facts - **What**: Real estate sales in the Canton of Bern (procedures and taxation on three levels) - Where: Canton Bern, central Switzerland - Who: Buyers, Swiss banks (regulated by FINMA), notaries public, Cantonal Administration Bern - Own funds: Minimum 20% (10% eligible with additional mortgage insurance) - Notary fees: 0.1%-0.3% of the purchase price - Cantonal taxes: They depend on the specific legislation of the Canton of Bern - Typical mortgage term: 15-20 years, with the possibility of extension
Buying a house in the Canton of Bern means interfacing with a regulatory system on three levels: federal (civil law, VAT), cantonal (transfer taxes, registration fees) and municipal (additional local taxes). Unlike other European countries, there is no single federal tax on the transfer of real estate in Switzerland; each canton establishes its own rates, calculation bases and procedures.
## How the mortgage loan works
Swiss banks-regulated by the Federal Financial Market Supervisory Authority FINMA-erogano mortgage loans for the purchase of residential homes. [Quando cerchi un mutuo presso una banca svizzera](nav:banks), you'll find that the ## Taxation at Federal, Cantonal, and Municipal Levels
At the federal level, VAT (standard rate 7.7% in Switzerland) applies to services related to the transaction (notarial consultation, administrative registration), but NOT to the transfer itself of residential real estate property. This is one of the aspects that distinguishes real estate transactions from the sale of movable goods or ordinary services.
At the cantonal level, the Canton of Bern applies a property transfer tax (also called 'real estate mutation rights' or 'registration tax'): this is a tax on the transfer of property, usually calculated as a percentage of the purchase price. Rates, exemptions, brackets, and procedures are specific to Bern cantonal legislation and vary significantly compared to other Swiss cantons (for example Zurich, Geneva, St. Gallen).
At the municipal level, some Bernese municipalities add additional registration rights to the cantonal tax. The Swiss federal system grants cantons broad fiscal autonomy: for this reason, the overall tax burden on real estate purchases varies considerably from one region of Switzerland to another.
## Mortgage Sustainability: Practical Scenarios
The sustainability of a mortgage depends on the buyer's income, the mortgage term, and current market interest rates. Swiss banks generally apply this sustainability criterion: debt service (principal + monthly interest) must not exceed 33% of the buyer's annual gross income.
With this rule, those with more modest annual income will see the maximum amount of mortgage they can request limited. Conversely, those with higher income will have greater financing capacity. The mortgage term significantly affects sustainability: a 15-year mortgage has higher monthly payments than a 20-year one, but produces less interest overall. A 25-30 year mortgage has lower payments, but higher total interest.
## How to Address Initial Costs
Anyone buying a home in the Canton of Bern faces significant initial costs beyond the base purchase price. These include: notarial fees (0.1%-0.3% of the price), [cantonal and municipal property transfer taxes](nav:calculator) (percentage variable according to Bern legislation), property insurance against fire and damage (mandatory, premiums vary by location and property characteristics), and supplementary mortgage insurance (if own funds are below 20%, additional insurance is required with a premium usually paid as a lump sum).
Careful planning, including a tax estimate from the competent Bern cantonal office for real estate taxes, is essential before signing the purchase agreement. Many buyers rely on a notary or professional real estate consultant to calculate the total final costs and verify the overall sustainability of the transaction.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## Step-by-Step Procedure
Anyone deciding to purchase a property in Canton Bern should follow this operational sequence:
1. Preliminary assessment of financial capacity Before looking for a specific property, contact a Swiss bank directly (your main bank or other credit institutions) for a financing pre-assessment. The bank examines your income, existing debts, and available personal funds, expressing the maximum mortgage amount it is willing to provide.
2. Property search and purchase promise Once a property of interest is found, the seller (or the appointed real estate agent) signs a bilateral purchase promise, which binds both parties to proceed towards the purchase. The promise specifies the agreed price, conditions (property condition, included systems), the expected date for signing before the notary, and any cancellation clauses.
3. Formal mortgage request to the bank Submit the financing request to the bank with an attached copy of the purchase promise, your income statement (last 2-3 years), banking documents, and allow the bank to conduct a technical appraisal of the property (or request it yourself directly). The appraisal typically takes 4-8 weeks.
4. Notary intervention and tax calculation Once the mortgage is confirmed in principle, the notary authenticates the deed of sale, calculates the taxes owed to Canton Bern and the specific municipality, and organizes the registration in the cantonal Land Register. The notary provides a written estimate of all final costs.
5. Payment of funds and cadastral registration On the agreed date, the purchaser pays the personal funds, the bank disburses the mortgage via bank transfer, and the notary proceeds with the definitive registration of the transfer of ownership in the Land Register. The final cadastral registration (final legal step) is completed within 1-3 months.
## Documents and information to collect
Before starting the procedure, gather in advance: - Copy of a valid identity document (passport or identity card) - Last three payslips or income statements - Income tax return for the last two years - Bank statements (last 3 months to prove availability of personal funds) - Complete list of your existing debts and loans (mortgages, personal loans, leasing) - Copy of the purchase promise (once signed)
## Where to turn for official information
**Swiss banks**: To simulate current interest rates, mortgage conditions and monthly payments, contact your credit institution directly or contact multiple banks to compare offers.
Canton Bern Land Registry Office: To verify the cadastral situation and the legitimacy of the property ownership, consult the Land Register.
Canton Bern Tax/Finance Office: To find out the exact amounts of transfer taxes, cantonal rates, exemptions, and any applicable exceptions or benefits.
Order of Notaries of Canton Bern: To obtain an official list of accredited public notaries and verify standard notarial fees.
For a complete and personalized estimate of all purchase costs, including federal, cantonal and municipal taxes, use the [Frontaliere Ticino tax calculator](nav:calculator), which takes into account updated Swiss tax legislation and allows you to simulate different purchase scenarios.

item.title: Asylum and crimes, the expert: prisons are not scary
item.description: Crime rate over 80% among asylum seekers from the Maghreb. According to expert Beat Stauffer, the causes are socio-economic and Swiss prisons have almost no deterrent effect.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Crime rate among asylum seekers from Maghreb exceeds 80% (SEM 2024 data) - Socio-economic causes, not cultural according to expert Beat Stauffer - Swiss prisons practically useless as a deterrent - Repatriations greatest deterrent, but procedures often fail
## Key Facts - **What**: Analysis of crime among asylum seekers from Maghreb - When: 2024, data from the State Secretariat for Migration - Where: Switzerland (federal asylum procedure) - Who: SEM and expert Beat Stauffer (10+ years in centers and prisons) - Percentages: 80% overall, 90% Algerian applications rejected, 80.5% average Maghreb - Asylum probability: Less than 1% for many applicants
An accusation rate for crimes exceeding 80% among asylum seekers from the Maghreb: this is the 2024 data contained in an internal analysis by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM), taken up by the newspaper Blick and at the center of intense debate at the national level. Maghreb region expert Beat Stauffer did not hide his surprise: 'I am surprised and shocked,' he told colleagues at 24Heures.
Stauffer, however, offers a more nuanced interpretation. Among Algerian applicants whose asylum application had been rejected, the rate reached nearly 90%. The expert believes that, once their application was rejected, some acted as if they had nothing left to lose. The overall average for all Maghreb countries, including also people whose asylum procedure is still ongoing, stands at around 80.5%.
A relevant figure for the debate on migration in Switzerland: this is not a marginal phenomenon, but a trend involving tens of thousands of people according to SEM statistics. Stauffer's analysis rules out easy explanations. 'It is not about cultural or religious factors. Young Maghrebis are often culturally closer to Europe compared to asylum seekers from other regions.'
### The decisive distinction: economic migrants vs. genuine applicants
According to Stauffer, the key interpretation lies in a fundamental distinction: 'These are economic migrants in irregular situations who, fundamentally, don't give a damn about the outcome of the asylum procedure. For those who truly hope to obtain asylum, committing a series of crimes while waiting would be counterproductive and irrational.' The rational calculation changes radically when the probability of protection drops below 1%. For those who don't believe in the procedure, the risk of legal consequences loses its deterrent force. [Discover how the cost of living in Switzerland affects the vulnerability of migrants](nav:cost-of-living). According to Stauffer's analysis, the causes of crime lie primarily in socio-economic factors rather than in cultural or religious elements. The explanation has its roots in material conditions: 'Poverty and precariousness have become alarming'. Many young people known as 'harraga' come from unfortunate families and contexts marked by violence and abandonment from childhood. 'They were confronted with violence and abandonment very early on. These young people have lost faith in their own State, as well as hope that one day the situation may improve for their generation'.
To this material desperation is added a deep distrust towards public institutions and the absence of concrete prospects. Stauffer further emphasizes how social networks contribute to feeding an illusory image of Europe, built around cars, parties, freedom and easy money. Yet, even knowing they have less than 1% chance of obtaining asylum, many still decide to leave. The gap between the expectations created by digital communication and the reality on the ground generates frustration, which in some cases leads to illegal behaviour.
### The practically zero deterrent effect of Swiss prisons
A crucial element emerges from the analysis on criminal deterrence. 'The deterrent effect of a Swiss prison is practically zero compared to that of a North African prison', states Stauffer. The expert cites a concrete case: an unaccompanied minor asylum seeker, after a few days in prison for an offence, did not want to return to the reception centre because they had not found the detention conditions particularly harsh. Furthermore, those who commit minor offences against property rarely end up in pre-trial detention, further reducing the deterrent effect.
Far more deterrent would be the prospect of repatriation. Returning to one's own country without money and without documents would represent a strong source of shame towards one's family — a cultural element that is far from marginal. However, repatriations often fail due to structural problems in identification. False personal details or inaccurate information about place of birth can make it difficult to obtain the necessary documents from consulates, with procedures that can take a year or more. This bureaucratic failure also undermines the most powerful deterrent identified by the expert. [Discover legal migration opportunities and employment integration programs in Switzerland](nav:jobs).
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). Stauffer, who taught for over ten years in Swiss asylum centers and prisons, also highlights the consequences of this situation for citizens originally from the Maghreb who live legally in Switzerland. In his view, many suffer from the negative image associated with the behavior of some of their compatriots and from the damage to the reputation of a region also known for its hospitality and cultural heritage. The entire legitimate Maghrebi community suffers the consequences, beyond the personal responsibility of each individual.
As for possible solutions, the expert does not propose simple and immediate answers. The numbers explain the complexity: one million young people would have abandoned school in Tunisia over fifteen years, and among 2-2.5 million Moroccans between 15 and 30 years old, many find themselves without training or work. Stauffer's proposed path goes through closer cooperation with Maghreb countries, through investments in facilities for street children and in vocational training. Beyond that, there would need to be an opening of legal channels for labor migration, which would allow young Maghrebis to seek income opportunities in a regular manner.
### International Cooperation and Current Obstacles
In return, Stauffer argues, North African governments should guarantee the readmission of their citizens without bureaucratic obstacles, speeding up the identification and documentation processes that today make forced deportations ineffective. The proposal is not purely theoretical: it requires bilateral investments in vocational training in countries of origin, creation of local employment opportunities, and, above all, a redefinition of migration channels from 'illegal' to 'regulated'. A migration policy based on prevention and cooperation, rather than on repression and incarceration, could address at the root the socio-economic drivers that fuel the phenomenon observed in the 2024 data. The announcement by USI and SUPSI about the increase in university fees sparked political protests in the Canton of Ticino. On August 25, 2026, the Movement for Socialism immediately protested, defining the choice as "political" and not "inevitable". According to MPs, universities have passed on the cost of federal and cantonal cuts directly to students and their families, rather than publicly contesting the cuts and claiming the resources needed for training.
The Independent Union of Students and Apprentices (SISA) added to the criticism, noting that "Ticino university fees have long been well above the Swiss average". Although universities promise “fair and inclusive access”, SISA fears that the new amounts ### The transfer of costs to students
The heart of the protest lies in the mechanism through which the Canton of Ticino faces the budget crisis. Rather than supporting public funding of university education, the cantonal and local administrations shifted the economic burden directly to students' families. The Movement for Socialism contests that this choice represents "the definition of public education". The MPs argues that there are "other ways": defending public funding, questioning cuts or "finding new resources through more redistributive taxation".
This transfer of costs is particularly significant considering that the cantonal cuts are part of the project called "10% initiative", linked to the implementation of sick cash subsidies (LAMal) at the cantonal level. In other words, federal social policy decisions end up directly impacting access to higher education at the regional level. According to the MPs, the universities "could have challenged the cuts and claimed the resources necessary for training, instead of intervening on the easier front"-that is, transferring the problem to family budgets.

Ticino students find themselves in a vulnerable position. An increase in university tuition is not an abstract matter of budgeting, but a reality that impacts concrete family decisions. For families just above the thresholds for access to cantonal subsidies (calculated using federal criteria similar to those of the LAMal), an annual increase of hundreds of francs per child in education entails difficult choices: postponing education, seeking work parallel to studies, or abandoning academic aspirations.

### Political Divergences
The debate is deeply ideological. The Movement for Socialism argues that public funding of education is a collective good, and that the cuts represent a 'political choice' to downsize the welfare state. SISA does not directly oppose the right of universities to modify tuition, but calls for concrete guarantees that the promise of 'equitable and inclusive access' remains real and is concretized 'in support measures for students who cannot afford such amounts'. item.title: Secretary of State for Climate: the Greens' request
item.description: The Greens call for a Secretary of State for Climate and Exit from Fossil Energies. Lisa Mazzone attacks Federal Councillor Rösti head-on.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Greens call for Secretary of State for Climate Protection and Exit from Fossils - Lisa Mazzone accuses Rösti: not suitable to lead the climate transition - Switzerland will not reach 2030 climate targets, admits Federal Council
## Key facts - **What**: Creation of the Secretary of State for Climate Protection - Who: Green Party, Lisa Mazzone (president), Albert Rösti (federal councillor) - When: 2026, during a heat wave - Where: Swiss federal level - Amount: 8 billion francs ends up abroad each year for fossil fuels - Objective: Planned exit from fossil fuels by 2030
The Green Party no longer accepts slow times on climate policy. During a press conference, Lisa Mazzone, president of the party, announced a double request to the Federal Council: the creation of a Secretary of State dedicated to climate protection and a commitment to a planned exit from fossil fuels.
But the most direct message is addressed to Federal Councillor Albert Rösti. Mazzone accuses him head-on of not being the right person to act with the necessary determination on the climate. He explicitly asked the Federal Council to remove the Department of the Environment from him. The reason? According to the president of the Greens, Rösti continues to deny the severity of the climate crisis, remaining tied to his own dogmas and lobbies.
The heaviest figure comes from a statement that Fossil energy dependency numbers tell a story that directly affects the portfolios of Swiss residents. According to Marionna Schlatter, national councilor of the Greens of the Canton of Zurich, every year 8 billion francs ends up abroad, fueling both the climate crisis and international conflicts. These are resources that, if reinvested in Switzerland, could finance climate adaptation and internal energy transition.
This is where the Buildings Programme comes into play, a federal instrument that the Greens want to strengthen financially and also extend to measures against heat. The program is aimed at rehabilitating existing buildings to reduce CO₂ emissions while improving protection from excessive heat. The logic is simple: with the same investment, two problems are solved at the same time. Less energy consumption for winter heating, less need for air conditioning in summer, less emissions, less weight on the bill.
### What it really means for people living in Switzerland
For property owners and renters, a possible expansion of the Buildings Program would entail access to federal contributions, often coupled with cantonal incentives, for renovation work and thermal insulation. Cantons such as Ticino, Valais, Vaud and Geneva already offer complementary subsidies to federal programs. A dedicated Secretary of State could accelerate the integration between the

The Greens' request will follow Swiss constitutional channels. A State Secretary for climate protection requires a parliamentary initiative—a motion or postulate—presented by one or more green deputies, followed by discussion in federal Commissions, then in Plenary. The process is not fast: from a proposal to a vote in the Chamber, months or even years can pass, depending on the order of parliamentary business.
The request to remove Albert Rösti from the Department of the Environment is a strong political statement, but which, constitutionally, cannot be imposed by a motion: the Federal Council appoints the ministers, and Parliament elects the Federal Council as a collegial body. What the Greens can do is fuel public and parliamentary debate on climate policy management, influence the agenda of the Chambers, and resort to procedures such as interpellations and oral questions to oversee the work of the Department of the Environment.
### How to follow the political process
Swiss citizens can consult the Federal Parliament website (parlament.ch) to track the evolution of green motions, read official documents, and discover how their representatives vote. Many cantons have similar platforms for cantonal parliament. For those living in Ticino or other regions, it is also useful to follow cantonal debates on energy and climate, since cantons have concurrent powers with the Confederation on building, urban planning, and part of energy policy. The State Secretary for climate protection, if established, would have the task of coordinating the energy transition between the various federal Departments and ensuring that political decisions respect the objective of exiting fossil fuels. This entails periodic reviews of federal subsidies to fossil fuels, alignment of tax policy on VAT and fuels to climate targets, and coordination with cantonal initiatives.

item.title: Expensive petrol and diesel, but oil goes down
item.description: Despite the 28% drop in oil prices, it is increasingly expensive to fill up in Switzerland. Petrol at 2.13 CHF/litre, diesel at 2.27 CHF/litre: the increase has exceeded 40 cents since February.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Oil down 28%, fuels up in Switzerland - Petrol 2.13 CHF/litre, diesel 2.27 CHF/litre - Destroyed refineries reduce global supply by 10% - River transport 10 times more expensive for lower Rhine
## Key facts - **What**: Fuel prices paradoxically increasing - When: August 2026 vs February 2026 - Where: Switzerland (TCS data) - Who: Swiss Touring Club, AWP experts - Petrol: 2.13 CHF per litre - Diesel: CHF 2.27 per litre - Increase: Over 40 cents since February - Cause: Global refinery crisis (-10% capacity)
### The Swiss pump paradox
Despite the fact that the price of a barrel of crude oil has fallen by 28% compared to the maximum reached at the beginning of May, filling up in Switzerland is costing more and more. It is a paradox that worries motorists and that, according to experts, is due to deep structural reasons, linked above all to the destruction of refineries in theaters of war in the Middle East and Ukraine.
Data from the Swiss Touring Club (TCS) confirm the rise in price: the average price for a liter of unleaded 98 gasoline reached 2.13 francs, while diesel is sold at 2.27 francs. At the end of February, the same fuels cost CHF 1.78 and CHF 1.79 respectively. In a few months, therefore, the price increased by more than 40 cents per litre.
Two converging factors explain this anomaly. The first is exceptional and, over time, should be attenuated: the heatwave has drastically reduced the ### Switzerland's vulnerability
For Switzerland, which depends on imports for approximately 70-75% of its petroleum product needs, the situation is particularly difficult. The only national refinery, located in Cressier in Canton Neuchâtel, operates at full capacity but is completely integrated into European supply chains and cannot make up for the deficit. Most fuel arrives by ship via the Rhine, making the country vulnerable to both logistical and structural problems.
This depends not on recent choices, but on Swiss geography and industrial structure. Increasing refining capacity in Europe or Switzerland appears as a prohibitive operation, which would require enormous investments and long timeframes. For this reason, specialists consulted by AWP predict that the situation will remain tense for a long time.
For those who work on the road — transporters, representatives, technicians — the impact is immediate: profit margins erode. A [car cost calculator](nav:calculator) can help assess the precise economic effect.
### Limited prospects in the short to medium term
Although transport costs may decrease in the medium term — when the Rhine returns to normal levels — as long as current bottlenecks persist in world refineries, Swiss motorists will hardly be able to expect real relief at the pump.
The economic impact is broad: even for commuters who cross the national territory, operating costs rise significantly. The situation is complicated by the fact that, unlike previous energy crises (such as the 2022 one that affected the entire world), this time the factor is distributed: part depends on Swiss river logistics (which can improve), part from uncontrollable geopolitical factors (refinery destruction). This combination makes a quick solution very difficult.
An important aspect is also the inflationary context: higher fuel costs are reflected in freight transport costs, and therefore in the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) in general. It's not just a matter of the pump, but a cascading effect on the entire economy.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Concrete strategies to address high prices
While waiting for the situation to improve, Swiss motorists can adopt several concrete strategies. The first is to optimize fuel consumption through less aggressive driving: gradual accelerations, constant speed, regular vehicle maintenance.
The second is to evaluate alternatives: [public transport](nav:transport) often remains more cost-effective compared to the total costs of owning and managing a private car. For those who have the possibility, carpooling (sharing the ride with colleagues or friends) reduces fuel costs spread across more people. In the medium term, electric vehicles could offer economic advantages, although the initial purchase cost is higher.
It is also useful to regularly monitor prices at the pump: the TCS publishes average data by canton, and in some cases it is possible to find gas stations with slightly lower rates. Filing a tax return, for its part, allows those who have incurred fuel expenses for professional reasons (representatives, craftsmen, freelancers with frequent travel) to deduct the expenses from taxable income.
### What to monitor in the coming months
The level of the Rhine will continue to be a critical indicator. When water returns to normal levels, the cost of shipping via ship should decrease significantly. This could lead to a reduction of 10-20 cents per liter in the second half of the year, if geopolitical factors do not worsen further.
In the meantime, it is important to keep an eye on the evolution of global refineries and the conflicts affecting them. Although Italy and France have greater refining capacity than Switzerland, and can theoretically supply fuel to the Swiss market via pipeline, the profit margin of the refineries themselves remains high as long as their global capacity is limited.
For those planning car purchases or investments, fuel prices should remain in the calculation of operating costs for some more months. Consulting a [car cost calculator](nav:calculator) can help estimate the economic impact of a new vehicle.

## In a nutshell - In the canton of Zurich there is a progressive cantonal and municipal inheritance tax - Spouse and direct descendants benefit from significant tax protections - The declaration must comply with strict deadlines established by the cantonal administration - The Swiss tax system is divided into three levels: federal, cantonal and municipal
## Key facts - **What**: Inheritance and gift tax at cantonal level in Zurich - Where: Canton Zurich (responsibility of the cantonal tax administration) - When: Declaration within the deadlines established by the tax office - Who: Heirs and recipients of donations - Structure: Three tax levels (federal, cantonal, municipal)
In the Canton of Zurich, as in all Swiss regions, inheritance tax represents a tax lever with exclusive cantonal competence. The Zurich cantonal regime applies a progressive system of inheritance taxation, with tiers differentiated according to the degree of kinship of the beneficiary with the deceased.
The Swiss tax system operates on three distinct levels: federal, cantonal and municipal. For inheritance tax, jurisdiction is entirely cantonal and municipal-there is no federal inheritance tax. This means that each canton legislates autonomously on rates, exemptions and procedures, creating a diverse tax landscape across regions. The Canton of Zurich defines its own rules at the cantonal level; the municipalities ### Inheritance and Franchises for Spouse and Descendants
In the Canton of Zurich, as in Swiss succession systems, the law provides for differentiated treatments depending on the degree of kinship between the beneficiary and the deceased. The surviving spouse generally benefits from significant tax protections, often up to complete exemption from inheritance tax when inheriting from the deceased partner. This legislative choice reflects the intention to preserve family unity during the critical patrimonial transition that follows death.
For direct descendants (children), the cantonal system often provides personal franchises—amounts below which the inheritance is not taxed—and reduced rates on the excess. This structure is consistent with the intention to favor intergenerational transfer of family wealth.
Differently, for more distant relatives (brothers, cousins) and non-relatives, protections decrease and higher rates apply. This gradation reflects the Swiss policy choice to encourage patrimonial conservation within the tight family nucleus.
### Donations Mortis Causa and Donations Inter Vivos
In Swiss law, donations are divided into two categories: donations mortis causa (testamentary transfers) and donations inter vivos (transfers made by the donor during their lifetime). The Canton of Zurich applies distinct tax regimes for the two categories.
It is common for donations inter vivos to benefit from special exemptions or reduced rates compared to succession, in order to encourage voluntary transfer during life. However, cantonal administrations reserve the right to review them if suspected of being made close to death with the purpose of evading inheritance taxes.
For accurate tax planning, it is advisable to consult a specialized consultant familiar with the current Zurich cantonal regulations.
### Scenarios of Differential Taxation
The Zurich tax system differentiates burdens according to the degree of kinship. A hypothetical scenario illustrates the contrast: when a spouse inherits from the deceased partner, the transfer generally benefits from special protections. When a daughter inherits from her father, she accesses franchises and reduced rates on the excess. When a non-related stranger inherits an equivalent amount, they do not access the same protections and tax burdens are significantly higher.
This structuring reflects the Swiss principle of preserving patrimonial transfer within the family nucleus, a principle consistent across all cantons maintaining an inheritance tax. For specific calculations on your inheritance situation, use our [tax calculator](nav:calculator). ### Inheritance Declaration: Procedure When a person dies in the Canton of Zurich, the heirs have the obligation to notify the cantonal tax administration within the time limits set by cantonal law. The procedure follows specific steps defined by Zurich regulations.
Step 1 – Death Notification. The heirs or the executor (if designated) must notify the cantonal tax office within the time limits. The notification must include the deceased's personal data and a preliminary list of designated beneficiaries.
Step 2 – Filing the Declaration. The cantonal tax administration provides official forms for the inheritance declaration. The form must include a complete inventory of the estate (real estate, bank accounts, securities, debts), the name and degree of kinship of each heir, and the gross value of the inheritance.
Step 3 – Attachment of Documentation. The declaration must be attached to certificates of death, will (if in authentic form), cadastral certificates, bank account extracts, the deceased's previous year tax returns, and any document that justifies the valuation of the inherited assets.
Step 4 – Payment of Tax. Once the cantonal tax notice is issued, the total amount must be paid within the indicated time limit. Failure to pay on time incurs late payment interest and potential enforcement actions.
### Deadlines and Administrative Terms The deadlines for the inheritance declaration in the Canton of Zurich are mandatory and set by cantonal law. The declaration must be submitted within a defined period—typically 30-90 days from the death, depending on the applicable cantonal regulations. It is essential to consult the official website of the cantonal tax administration to verify the exact deadlines and download the updated forms.
Delays in submission incur administrative penalties and accumulation of late payment interest. It is therefore crucial to notify the death promptly and complete the [inheritance declaration within the communicated deadlines](nav:tax-return).
### Available Tools and Resources The cantonal tax administration of Zurich makes available downloadable official forms, telephone and in-person consultation at cantonal offices, as well as support from notaries with specific expertise in Swiss inheritance.
To estimate the approximate amount of inheritance tax based on the value of the inheritance and the degree of kinship, use our [tax calculator](nav:calculator). For specific details regarding your situation (exact rates, applicable exemptions, special procedures), contact the cantonal tax office of your place of residence or a tax consultant affiliated with the cantonal tax administration.

## In a nutshell - The AVS is the first pillar of Swiss social security, fuelled by mandatory contributions of 5.3% for employees - The cantonal compensation fund manages contributions and annuities in the territory - Contribution gaps directly reduce the final monthly AVS income - Supplementary benefits provide a safety net for those with insufficient income
## Key facts - **What**: Pillar social security system with AVS as mandatory basis - Employee contribution: 5.3% of gross salary (10.6% with employer share) - Management: Cantonal compensation fund for collection and disbursement - Contribution gaps: Years without payments proportionally reduce the income - Complementary benefits: Monthly integration to cover the minimum living - Reference age: 64 years old women, 65 years old men
The Swiss social security system is divided into three pillars. The AVS, the first pillar, is the mandatory basis: each employee pays 5.3% of the salary, to which is added an equivalent contribution from the employer (overall 10.6% on the paycheck). Self-employed workers also pay contributions calculated on their professional income.
The canton's compensation fund collects these payments and manages the related benefits. It is not a personal deposit in which money remains frozen: it is an administrative institution that works with solidarity principles, where the contributions of those who work finance the income of ### How the clearinghouse is structured
The cantonal clearing house (as in every Swiss canton) is the entity that centralizes the management of the AVS at the territorial level. It receives payments from companies and self-employed workers, maintains individual tax registers, calculates pensions upon reaching the reference age (64 for women, 65 for men), and pays monthly payments to pensioners.
The cashier is NOT a bank where your money remains deposited in a personal account — it is a public administration that distributes the collected social security wealth according to federal rules and the principle of solidarity between generations. Each canton has its own compensation fund, often managed by the cantonal department of social insurance or the finance office.
### The calculation of the annuity: components and variability
The AVS annuity is not a simple reimbursement of the deposit. It is calculated on the basis of three main components:
1. **Years of contribution**: the completeness of the working career (ideally 44 years for the maximum income). Those who have gaps receive a proportionately lower income.
2. Average Salary: The average income reported during the career, discounted according to federal indices. Not only the final salary counts, but the entire work history, which makes it important to verify the correctness of the recorded data.
3. Contribution gaps: every year without
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Verify your rights: a step-by-step guide
If you are approaching the reference age (64-65 years) or want to check your AVS rights, follow these concrete steps:
1. Request your career extract (Versicherungsverlauf) Contact your cantonal compensation fund or visit the Federal Social Insurance Office (UFAS, German UFAS, French OFAS) website. The extract shows all registered payments, gaps, the duration of the accredited career, and personal data as recorded in federal archives. It's free and can be requested online or by mail.
2. Calculate an estimate of your pension Many cantons and the UFAS offer online calculators where you insert the extract data and receive a projection of your future AVS pension. This estimate is useful for planning your retirement and understanding if integration with other income sources (LPP, third pillar) will be necessary.
3. Evaluate the appeal for unjustified gaps If you discover unjustified gaps (periods where you would have had to pay but it's not recorded), you can appeal within a limited term (usually 1-2 years) to fill or correct them. Some periods of illness, unemployment with benefits, or other events may be covered by equity contributions - check with the fund.
**4. Plan the third pillar If the pension estimate seems insufficient, consider contributions to a [third pillar 3a account](nav:pillar3) up to the annual maximum (variable amount, check with your bank each year). This integrates your AVS and reduces federal, cantonal, and municipal taxation.
### How to request complementary benefits
In the 3-6 months before accessing your pension (don't wait for the first day of pension), contact: - Cantonal office for complementary benefits: in the Canton of Zurich, consult the official cantonal website and search for "complementary AVS/AI benefits" - Your place of residence: many municipalities handle local procedures in coordination with the canton
Required documents (typical list, check with the canton): - Official cantonal request form (downloadable from the cantonal website) - Last AVS career extract - Asset documentation (bank statements, property certificates, life insurance policies with surrender value) - Current income documentation (if still working or have other sources) - Rental contract or property certificate - Residency certificate
The processing time varies (usually 2-3 months), so it's a good idea to start the procedure in advance.

item.title: Apprenticeship in the canton of Inner Appenzell
item.description: Practical guide: how to find an internship, enter into the contract, understand salary and professional maturity in the Inner Appenzell Canton.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The apprenticeship in Switzerland lasts 3-4 years combining business training (70%) and vocational school (30%) - In the Inner Appenzell Canton, federal regulations and cantonal ordinances on training apply - The apprentice is entitled to a written contract, minimum wage (if set in canton), minimum holiday of 4 weeks - Conclusion with certificate of internship or additional professional maturity
## Key facts - **What**: Dual vocational training system (apprenticeship) - When: After compulsory school, usually from 15-16 years old - Where: Company (practical training) + Cantonal vocational school - Who: Apprentice, trainee teacher, vocational school, employer - Duration: 3-4 years depending on the professional profile - Regulation: Federal Code of Obligations (art. 344-346) + cantonal ordinances
In the Inner Appenzell Canton, as in all Swiss cantons, apprenticeship represents the main path towards a nationally recognized professional qualification. The system works according to the federal dual model: the young person works in a company for about 70% of his time and attends the cantonal vocational school for the remaining 30%, thus guaranteeing both theoretical and practical skills.
Apprenticeship is governed by federal law (Code of Obligations, articles 344-346) and by the cantonal ordinances of the Inner Appenzell Canton. The duration depends on the chosen professional profile and is ### Compensation and Social Contributions of the Apprentice
The compensation varies significantly depending on the professional sector and the year of apprenticeship attended. In the first year, an apprentice typically earns between 30-50% of the salary of a qualified worker in the same profession; in subsequent years, the compensation increases progressively, often following salary curves defined by sectoral collective contracts or specific cantonal ordinances.
In the Canton of Appenzello Interno, as in other cantons, the main sectors (agriculture, commerce, craftsmanship, industry, services) have publicly available remuneration tables at the cantonal office of education or professional associations. These amounts are binding for the apprenticeship contract.
From the apprentice's gross salary, various mandatory social contributions at the federal level are deducted:
- AVS/AI (Old Age and Disability Insurance): 5.3% of the gross salary (the employer also pays 5.3%, total 10.6%) - Unemployment insurance (AD/AC): 1.1% up to the annual maximum established - Health insurance (LAMal): the apprentice must conclude it autonomously within 3 months from the start (mandatory for residents), with premiums varying by canton and by choice of deductible - Work accident insurance (LAINF): managed and financed by the employer (contribution of 0.7-1.5% depending on the sector), part of the invisible labor cost in the pay slip - LPP (Professional Old-Age Insurance): not always applicable to apprentices, but in certain sectors or larger employers, contributions are provided on a percentage of the salary coordinated
The AVS, unemployment, and LAMal contributions are deducted directly from the pay slip. Consult your [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate how much will remain net after all deductions.
To deepen the functioning of Swiss social security (AVS, LPP, third pillar), you can consult our [guide to pension and social security](nav:pension).
### Professional Maturity: Path and Opportunities
Professional maturity is a post-apprenticeship diploma that allows direct access to the Swiss tertiary cycle, including secondary schools, universities of applied sciences, and master's degrees. It is a different and higher title than the ordinary apprenticeship certificate.
In the Canton of Appenzello Interno, professional maturity is offered by the cantonal professional school and can be pursued through two paths:
1. Integrated professional maturity: attended during the apprenticeship (1-2 additional days a week beyond regular school), allowing the diploma at the end of the apprenticeship 2. Specialized professional maturity: attended after completing the apprenticeship, in a dedicated 1-2 year additional path
Candidates must pass written exams in general subjects (German, mathematics, history, sciences, foreign languages) and related subjects to the professional profile. The professional maturity certificate is issued by the canton and recognized at the national level, opening doors to careers in higher education and the qualified labor market.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step procedure for applying for an internship
Phase 1: Explore available professional profiles Consult the complete federal catalogue of training profiles on berufsberatung.ch (managed by SECO) and the cantonal portal of the Appenzell Innerrhoden Office of Vocational Training. Identify 3-5 professions that match your interests and abilities. Access detailed descriptions of tasks, sectors, and required skills.
Phase 2: Prepare the application dossier Write a clear and concise curriculum vitae in German (official language of the canton), a motivation letter addressed to the chosen employer, copies of the last two school reports certifying your performance, and language proficiency certificates (if required by the sector). Some sectors (e.g. healthcare, public services) may require a physical fitness certificate or a background check.
Phase 3: Identify companies in Appenzell Innerrhoden Contact artisanal, manufacturing, agricultural, and service companies directly that operate in your area of interest. The canton has trade associations and industrial associations that provide updated lists and addresses of companies. Ask for information by phone before sending the dossier.
Phase 4: Send applications and participate in interviews Send your dossier via email or in person, attaching the cantonal internship application form (available at the Office of Vocational Training). The selected companies will contact you for an interview. Be punctual, professional, and ready to describe your motivations and expectations.
**Phase 5: Sign the contract If the interview outcome is positive, the company will propose a preliminary internship contract. Read all clauses carefully, check the remuneration, working hours, school days, and rights. Sign the contract within 4 weeks before the planned start date, usually in August or September.
### Deadlines and calendars for 2026 - Research: start 1-2 years before completing compulsory school (around 13-14 years old) - Applications: usually from September to March of the previous year - Sign contract: by April for a September start - Internship start: generally in August/September (canton calendar) - Final exam: in the last 3 months of the internship - Release certificate: within 30 days of passing the final exam
### Official resources in Appenzell Innerrhoden - Office of Vocational Training: consultation, company addresses, school calendars, official contract forms - School Career Guidance Office: support for students in choosing a profile and employer - Berufsberatung.ch portal: national catalogue of professions, job descriptions, training courses, companies - Regional artisanal and industrial associations: specific lists for sectors, networking events, information on minimum wages - SECO (Federal Department of Economy): federal regulations on vocational training and youth worker protection
### Tips for increasing chances of acceptance - Contact companies in advance: many select candidates 1-1.5 years before the planned start date - Attend orientation days, job fairs, and events organized by the canton - Request a short internship (1-2 weeks) at an interesting company to familiarize yourself with the sector and show motivation - Improve your German language skills (if not your native language): it's a common selection criterion - Maintain good grades in math, sciences, and language: many companies check these in school reports - Be prepared for the attitude test: some employers (especially in administration, healthcare, finance) administer it

Enter the sector, canton (Appenzell Innerrhoden), and internship year to receive an automatic estimate of the monthly net salary. This will help you evaluate if the proposed remuneration is competitive and adequate for your cost of living.
